'''James Joseph Sylvester''' (3 September 1814&nbsp;– 15 March 1897) was an [[United Kingdom|English]] [[mathematician]]. He made fundamental contributions to [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]], [[invariant theory]], [[number theory]], [[Integer partition|partition theory]], and [[combinatorics]].  He played a leadership role in American mathematics in the later half of the 19th century as a professor at the [[Johns Hopkins University]] and as founder of the ''[[American Journal of Mathematics]]''.  At his death, he was a professor at [[Oxford University]].

==Early life, family and education==
James Joseph was born in [[London]] on 3 September 1814, the son of Abraham Joseph, a [[Jews|Jewish]] merchant.<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|access-date=15 October 2018|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> James later adopted the surname ''Sylvester'' when his older brother did so upon emigration to the US. At age 14, Sylvester was a student of [[Augustus De Morgan]] at the University of London (now [[University College London]]). His family withdrew him from the university after he was accused of stabbing a fellow student with a knife. Subsequently, he attended the [[Liverpool Royal Institution]].

Sylvester began his study of mathematics at [[St John's College, Cambridge]] in 1831,<ref name="ACAD">{{acad|id=SLVR831JJ|name=Sylvester, James Joseph}}</ref> where his tutor was [[John Hymers]]. Although his studies were interrupted for almost two years due to a prolonged illness, he nevertheless ranked second in Cambridge's famous mathematical examination, the [[tripos]], for which he sat in 1837. However, Sylvester was not issued a degree, because graduates at that time were required to state their acceptance of the [[Thirty-nine Articles]] of the [[Church of England]], and he could not do so because he was Jewish. For the same reason, he was unable to compete for a Fellowship or obtain a [[Smith's prize]].<ref name="MenofMathematics">{{cite book | title=Men of Mathematics | publisher=Simon Schuster | author=Bell, Eric Temple | year=1986}}</ref> In 1838, Sylvester became professor of natural philosophy at [[University College London]] and in 1839 a Fellow of the Royal Society of London. In 1841, he was awarded a BA and an [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge and Dublin)|MA]] by [[Trinity College Dublin]]. 

==Career==
In 1841, Sylvester moved to the US to become a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Virginia]], the first Jewish professor at any American college or university.<ref name=Feuer>{{cite journal |last1=Feuer |first1=Lewis Samuel |title=America's First Jewish Professor: James Joseph Sylvester at the University of Virginia |journal=American Jewish Archives |date=1984 |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=152–201}}</ref> He left his appointment after only four months after a classroom incident in which a student he had criticized hit him with a bludgeon and he struck back with a sword-cane. The student collapsed in shock and Sylvester believed (wrongly) that he had killed him. Sylvester resigned when he felt that the university authorities had not sufficiently disciplined the student.{{r|Feuer}}<ref>{{cite web |url= https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Sylvester |title= Biography of Sylvester |website= mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk |publisher= MacTutor, [[University of St. Andrews]] |access-date= 2021-10-06}}</ref> He moved to New York City and began friendships with the Harvard mathematician [[Benjamin Peirce]]{{efn|Father of mathematician and philosopher [[Charles Sanders Peirce]]}} and the Princeton physicist [[Joseph Henry]]. However, he left in November 1843 after being denied appointment as Professor of Mathematics at Columbia College (now University), again for his Judaism, and returned to England.

In England, he was hired in 1844 by the [[Equity and Law Life Assurance Society]] for which he developed successful actuarial models and served as de facto CEO, a position that required a law degree. As a result, he studied for the Bar, meeting a fellow British mathematician studying law, [[Arthur Cayley]], with whom he made significant contributions to invariant theory and also [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]] during a long collaboration.<ref>{{Cite book | last1=Parshall | first1=Karen Hunger | title=James Joseph Sylvester. Jewish Mathematician in a Victorian world | url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=0801882915 | publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press | isbn=978-0-8018-8291-3 | year=2006 | mr=2216541}}</ref> He did not obtain a position teaching university mathematics until 1855, when he was appointed professor of mathematics at the [[Royal Military Academy, Woolwich]], from which he retired in 1869, because the compulsory retirement age was 55. The Woolwich academy initially refused to pay Sylvester his full pension, and only relented after a prolonged public controversy, during which Sylvester took his case to the letters page of ''[[The Times]]''.

In 1876,<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Preliminary Outline of Instructions for the Session Beginning October 3, 1876|date = September 1876|journal = Johns Hopkins University. Official Circulars |issue=5}}</ref> Sylvester returned to the US to become the inaugural professor of mathematics at the new [[Johns Hopkins University]] in [[Baltimore, Maryland]]. His salary was $5,000 (quite generous for the time), which he demanded be paid in gold, but after further negotiation, it was not.<ref name= hawkins>{{Cite book|title = Pioneer: A History of the Johns Hopkins University, 1874–1889|last = Hawkins|first = Hugh|publisher = Cornell University Press|year = 1960|location = Ithaca, New York|pages = 41–43}}</ref> 

Sylvester founded the ''[[American Journal of Mathematics]]'' in 1878.<ref name= Brittanica>{{cite encyclopedia |url= https://www.britannica.com/biography/James-Joseph-Sylvester |title= James Joseph Sylvester |encyclopedia= [[Encyclopedia Britannica]] |date= 2026-03-11 |access-date= 2026-05-14}}</ref> The only other mathematical journal in the US at that time was ''The Analyst'', which eventually became the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]''. Also in 1878, [[Christine Ladd-Franklin]] was accepted into [[Johns Hopkins University]] with his help. He remembered some of Ladd's earlier works in the ''Educational Times''.<ref name=Cadwallader>{{cite book |chapter=Christine Ladd-Franklin (1847-1930) |last1=Cadwallader |first1=J. V. |last2=Cadwallader |first2=T.C. |year=1990 |editor-first= A. N. |editor-last=O'Connell  |editor2-first= N. F. |editor2-last=Russo |title=Women in Psychology: A Bio-bibliographic Sourcebook |pages=220–225 |location=New York, NY |publisher=Greenwood Press }}</ref> Ladd's application for a fellowship was signed "C. Ladd", and the university offered her the position without realizing she was a woman.<ref name=Riddle>{{cite web |last=Riddle |first=Larry |title=Christine Ladd-Franklin |url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/ladd.htm |publisher=Agnes Scott College |access-date=6 November 2012}}</ref> When they did realise her gender, the board tried to revoke the offer, but Sylvester insisted that Ladd should be his student, and so she was.<ref name=Riddle/> She held a fellowship at Johns Hopkins University for three years, but the trustees did not allow her name to be printed in circulars with those of other fellows, for fear of setting a precedent.<ref name=Riddle/> Furthermore, dissension over her continued presence forced one of the original trustees to resign.<ref name=Riddle/>

In 1883, Sylvester returned to England to take up the position of [[Savilian Professor of Geometry]] at [[Oxford University]]. He held this chair until his death, although in 1892 the university appointed a deputy professor to the same chair. He was on the governing body of [[Abingdon School]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.abingdon.org.uk/uploads/school/files/abingdonian/1897_April_V002_N005.pdf#page=13|title=School Notes| work= The Abingdonian| via= abingdon.org.uk| access-date= }}</ref>

=== Concepts and terminology coined ===
Sylvester introduced a number of mathematical terms that remain in use. He coined the word "[[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]" in 1850,<ref>[http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/HistTopics/Matrices_and_determinants.html Matrices and determinants], The MacTutor History of Mathematics archive</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Sylvester | first=J.J. | date = November 1850|  title = Additions to the articles in the September Number of this Journal "On a new Class of Theorem" and "On Pascal's Theorem" |journal = London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine | volume =37 | pages = 363–369| doi=10.1080/14786445008646629 }}</ref> the term "[[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]" in the sense of ''network'',<ref>{{cite journal |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=KcoKAAAAYAAJ |title= Chemistry and algebra |last= Sylvester |first= J. J. |journal= Nature |date= 1878-02-07 |volume= 17 |page= [https://books.google.com/books?id=KcoKAAAAYAAJ&q=Sylvester&pg=PA284 284] |via= Google Books |quote= Every invariant and covariant thus becomes expressible by a ''graph'' precisely identical with a Kekuléan diagram or chemicograph. |access-date= }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=1q0EAAAAYAAJ |title= On an application of the new atomic theory to the graphical representation of the invariants and covariants of binary quantics, — with three appendices |last= Sylvester |first= J. J. |journal= American Journal of Mathematics, Pure and Applied |year= 1878 |volume= 1 |issue= 1 |pages= [https://books.google.com/books?id=1q0EAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA64 64–90] |via= Google Books |access-date= }} The term "graph" first appears in this paper on page 65.</ref> and the term "[[discriminant]]".<ref>{{cite journal |title= On a remarkable discovery in the theory of canonical forms and of hyperdeterminants |last= Sylvester |first= J. J. |journal= Philosophical Magazine |year= 1851 |publisher= 4th series |volume= 2 |pages = 391–410}} Sylvester coined the term "discriminant" on [https://books.google.com/books?id=DBNDAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA406 page 406].</ref> He also introduced the word "totient" for [[Euler's totient function]] φ(''n'').<ref>{{cite journal |title= On certain ternary cubic-form equations |last= Sylvester |first= J. J. |journal= American Journal of Mathematics |year= 1879 |volume= 2 |pages = 357–393}} Sylvester coins the term "totient" on [https://books.google.com/books?id=-AcPAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA361 page 361]:  "(the so-called ''Φ'' function of any number I shall here and hereafter designate as its ''τ'' function and call its Totient)"</ref>

In [[discrete geometry]], he is remembered for [[Sylvester–Gallai theorem|Sylvester's problem]] and a result on the [[orchard problem]], and in matrix theory he discovered [[Sylvester's determinant identity]],<ref>{{cite journal | last = Sylvester | first = James Joseph | title = On the relation between the minor determinants of linearly equivalent quadratic functions | journal = Philosophical Magazine | volume = 1 | year = 1851 | pages = 295–305}}</ref> which generalizes the ''Desnanot–Jacobi identity''.<ref>C.G.J. Jacobi, "De Formatione et Proprietatibus Determinantium", Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik, 22, 285–318 (1841)</ref> His collected scientific work fills four volumes.

==Honors and awards==
In 1861, Sylvester was elected an honorary member of the [[Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society]]<ref>''Memoirs and Proceedings of the Manchester Literary & Philosophical Society'', Series 4, Vol. 8, 1894.</ref> and in 1872, he finally received his B.A. and M.A. from Cambridge, having been denied the degrees due to his being a Jew.<ref name="ACAD" /> In 1877, he was elected as a member to the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History |url= https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?year=1877;smode=advanced;startDoc=21|access-date=2021-05-10|website=search.amphilsoc.org|archive-date=25 January 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230125053224/https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?year=1877;smode=advanced;startDoc=21|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1880, the [[Royal Society|Royal Society of London]] awarded Sylvester the [[Copley Medal]], its highest award for scientific achievement.

==Personal life and demise==
Sylvester never married and is not known to have had any children; biographical sources do not record any romantic relationships.<ref>{{cite book |last=Parshall |first=Karen Hunger |title= James Joseph Sylvester: Jewish Mathematician in a Victorian World |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-8018-8291-3 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=6xNIAAAAIAAJ| via= Google Books |access-date=14 May 2026}}</ref> Throughout his career, he formed lasting friendships with leading scientific figures. In New York he became close to the mathematician Benjamin Peirce and the physicist Joseph Henry,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Feuer |first=Lewis Samuel |title=America's First Jewish Professor: James Joseph Sylvester at the University of Virginia |journal=American Jewish Archives |date=1984 |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=152–201 |url= https://americanjewisharchives.org/publications/journal/PDF/1984_36_02_00_feuer.pdf |access-date=14 May 2026}}</ref> and in England he developed a long and productive friendship with Arthur Cayley, with whom he shared both personal ties and major mathematical collaborations.<ref>{{cite book |last=Parshall |first=Karen Hunger |title=James Joseph Sylvester: Jewish Mathematician in a Victorian World |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-8018-8291-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6xNIAAAAIAAJ |access-date=14 May 2026}}</ref>

One of Sylvester's lifelong passions was for poetry; he read and translated works from the original French, German, Italian, [[Latin]] and [[Greek language|Greek]], and many of his mathematical papers contain illustrative quotes from classical poetry. Following his early retirement, Sylvester published ''[[The Laws of Verse]]'', a book in which he attempted to codify a set of laws for [[prosody (poetry)|prosody]] in poetry.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Sylvester | first1=J. J. | title=The Laws of Verse, or, Principles of Versification Exemplified in Metrical Translations | year=1870 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TxNIAAAAIAAJ | publisher=Longmans, Green and Co.|location=London}}</ref>

Sylvester died at 5 [[Hertford Street]], London on 15 March 1897. He is buried in [[Balls Pond Road Cemetery]] on Kingsbury Road in London.<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh |isbn=0-902-198-84-X |url= https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|access-date=15 October 2018|archive-date=4 March 2016| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Legacy==
In 1901, [[Royal Society|Royal Society of London]] instituted the [[Sylvester Medal]] in his memory, to encourage mathematical research after his death in [[Oxford]].

Sylvester House, a portion of an undergraduate dormitory at [[Johns Hopkins University]], is named in his honour. Several professorships there are named in his honour also.
